query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing engineered nanoscale surface trenches on a refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) intermediate layer will reduce the interfacial thermal boundary resistance, thereby significantly enhancing its effective heat-transfer capability without degrading its high‐temperature structural integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk, single‐phase refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., one similar to (CrFeTiTa)70W30 or MoWTaTiZr) that currently functions as a thermal barrier/intermediate layer between tungsten plasma‐facing components and CuCrZr heat sinks.
generation.intervention: Apply a nanoscale surface nanopatterning process (for example, using focused ion beam milling or lithography) to create an array of sub-micron trenches across the alloy’s surface that contacts adjacent layers.
generation.conditions: The intervention is designed to operate under fusion divertor conditions, with service temperatures in the range of 500–1000 °C and under high heat flux along with moderate mechanical loading; the irradiation environment typical for plasma-facing regions is also assumed.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanopatterning increases the effective contact area at the interface without disrupting the bulk crystalline structure, so the high‐entropy alloy retains its excellent phase stability and mechanical strength.
generation.mechanism: By introducing controlled nanoscale trenches, the thermal boundary resistance is reduced through enhanced phonon and electron coupling at the interface. This modification minimizes interfacial scattering losses while preserving the bulk integrity and thereby improves overall heat-transfer capability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a conventionally finished (polished) RHEA intermediate layer, the nanopatterned layer is expected to exhibit a measurable reduction (on the order of a few multiples improvement) in thermal boundary resistance with maintained or even slightly improved mechanical resilience under high-temperature, high-heat-flux conditions.
generation.baseline: The current state-of-the-art intermediate layers are fabricated with unpatterned, smooth surfaces that have higher interfacial resistance, which limits heat flow between the plasma-facing tungsten and the lower-temperature CuCrZr heat sink.
generation.boundary: This intervention must not induce microcracking, excessive porosity, or other damage (e.g., chemical segregation at the patterned surface) that would compromise the alloy’s inherent irradiation or high-temperature mechanical properties; effects should persist over thermal cycling typical of reactor operations.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines findings from a study demonstrating that nanoscale interfacial trenching can reduce thermal boundary resistance in GaN/diamond systems (PMC11984094) and insights into the tunable phonon behavior in HEAs (PMC11369437). Whether similar gains can be achieved in a refractory HEA—given its distinct alloy chemistry and extreme service conditions—is uncertain and requires experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical high-entropy alloy intermediate layers. One set will undergo nanoscale surface patterning to create trenches, while the control set remains with a standard smooth finish. Integrate both sets into a simulated divertor module assembly (e.g., bonding the RHEA between tungsten and a CuCrZr heat sink). Subject the modules to high heat flux, controlled thermal cycling up to 1000 °C, and representative irradiation doses in a plasma simulation environment.
measurements: Thermal boundary resistance using time-resolved thermoreflectance or equivalent techniques.
Overall effective heat-transfer rate across the interface.
Mechanical integrity and microstructural stability assessed by SEM, TEM, and XRD before and after testing.
Performance comparison of yield strength and ductility through high-temperature tensile tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanopatterned intermediate layers do not show a statistically significant reduction in thermal boundary resistance and improvement in heat-transfer rates compared to the control, or if the nanopatterning leads to degradation in mechanical stability (e.g., initiation of microcracks or phase degradation) under the prescribed test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys composed of five or more primary elements in equal or nearly equal proportions of atoms. In the present study, the thermophysical properties of the CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy (HEA) were investigated by a molecular dynamics (MD) method at nanoscale. The effects of the content of individual elements on lattice thermal conductivity kp were revealed, and the results suggested that adjusting the atomic content can be a way to control the lattice thermal conductivity of HEAs. The effects of temperature on kp were investigated quantitively, and a power-law relationship of kp with T−0.419 was suggested, which agrees with previous findings. The effects of temperature and the content of individual elements on volumetric specific heat capacity Cv were also studied: as the temperature increases, the Cv of all HEAs slightly decreases and then increases. The effects of atomic content on Cv varied with the comprising elements. AbstractGaN high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs) on SiC substrates are the highest performing commercially available transistors for high-power, high-frequency applications. However, Joule self-heating limits the maximum areal power density, i.e., operating power is derated to ensure the lifetime of GaN-based devices. Diamond is attractive as a heat sink due to its record-high thermal conductivity combined with its high electrical resistivity. GaN-on-diamond devices have been demonstrated, bringing the diamond as close as possible to the active device area. The GaN/diamond interface, close to the channel heat source, needs to efficiently conduct high heat fluxes, but it can present a significant thermal boundary resistance (TBR). In this work, we implement nanoscale trenches between GaN and diamond to explore new strategies for reducing the effective GaN/diamond TBR (TBReff). A 3× reduction in GaN/diamond TBReff was achieved using this approach, which is consistent with the increased contact area; thermal properties were measured using nanosecond transient thermoreflectance (ns-TTR).
